en: Whenever battle fever seized him,
He shot forth like a bullet-snake;
Before the bloodthirsty hero’s courage,
The Kara-Kytai and the Shibee people
All halted together, leaving none behind.
He was a blazing red ember;
Külchoro, upheld by fortune,
Was a steel bullet against the foe.
He was a cap of black steel,
The glory of the countless Kyrgyz.
When a grievous enemy pressed hard,
When calamity struck with force,
He was a black-burning fire.
He was a cap of red steel,
The morning-star glory of these Kyrgyz.
When an encircling enemy overwhelmed us,
He was a fire burning crimson.
Now cruel death has entered his thoughts too;
He too is departing
For the land from which none return.
My heroic mother Kanykei,
Until the five Ram stars had set,
Nursed me through five watches of the road;
Until the six Morning Stars had set,
She circled me and fed me.
She emptied her stone-hard breasts
And widened her narrow womb.
She suffered anguish for my sake,
Fleeing Talas and wandering,
Her soles blistering on the stones,
Following the banks of great Keng-Kol,
Saying, “He is the nephew left by my prince,”
She fled away for my sake.
Calling her father Karakhan but a corpse,
Calling it a plain where no lark flies,
Saying, “He is the child who bears my blood,”
She made her grieving head a banner,
Put her dear life to the test,
Fled and wandered, hiding her secret;
Calling it a plain where no soul can live,
Saying, “I will sacrifice my poor life
For my lone child, solitary as a crow.”
My dear mother Kanykei,
Purest of those in flowing gowns,
Foremost of women in white headscarves,
Most graceful of those with long hair,
Noblest of womankind,
Beauty among the dark-complexioned,
Greatest of all created souls,
Fruit of the fearsome desert,
Mother of me, Semetey.
My radiant lady, my sanctuary,
The wife of renowned Manas,
My mother who gave me shelter.
By the command of God the Creator,
My steadfast mother has gone to see
The true abode from which none return;
My caravan-leading mother has gone to see it.
My guardian above my head,
My mother Kanykei has set out upon the journey.
United when we were no bigger than lice,
At the age appointed for me,
With no battle cry and no public tidings,
With no mullah to say “Amen,”
When our fathers first pledged us in marriage,
At the age appointed for me.
Six thousand horses at the head,
Drawing the gaze of the whole wide world;
Upon a gray horse bright as moonlight,
White cotton as broad as a yurt’s path
Was displayed upon its forelock.
A thousand red-tailed camels,
Their faces turned toward the qibla,
Were loaded with red gold and jewels
And made to kneel facing the pole star.
The mouth of every treasury
Was opened for Khan Akun;
Abundant wealth beyond all counting
Was scattered before Khan Akun.
If cast into water for forty years,
Not the slightest edge would spoil;
If soaked in water for eighty years,
It would spring back without rotting.
However grave the hardship,
Not the faintest edge would spoil;
Though it endured forty years of famine,
Not the slightest thread would tarnish.
Carpets gleaming like gold
Were spread in splendor.
Abundant wealth and countless livestock
Were bestowed upon the pledged in-laws.
Bowing in homage and feasting on fat,
With abundant wealth and myriad livestock,
The pledged in-laws opened their hands in blessing.
With my princely father Manas at their head,
Abundant riches filled the place.
Thus our father-in-law, Khan Akun,
Entered into this marriage alliance.
The aged father of the people,
Dear holy Koshoy,
Saying, “Between this world and the next
I shall stand as impartial judge,”
The saintly Koshoy arose.
Receiving the blessing of “Amen,”
Our forefather Bakai sealed the bond.
“Manas and Khan Akun—
These two are now in-laws;
The foundation of their kinship
Shall be known among so many people.
Here are heroes and khans;
All the discerning people are here.
Here are eloquent men of sound judgment,
And others who know the finest ways
Of marching against the foe.
We have heard it beforehand,” they said,
“And are satisfied by the words spoken.
Not only in this world, but in the next,
On the Judgment Day of Resurrection,
Khan Manas and Khan Akun
Shall remain inseparable in-laws;
Abundant wealth and myriad livestock
Have been laid between them as a pledge.
To this service that has been performed,
Great and small and elders—
We all have borne witness,” they said,
Recalling the words of truth.
“We will not say it a second way.
Before the true God, all of us,
Great and small and elders,
Will not suffer true disgrace.
These are sufficient words, O hero.
Whoever denies them
Will have both cheeks blackened with soot;
If the words of one who turns away
Are accepted as true,
Can a human beast know wisdom?
Is he an infidel standing between us?
For twisting these words,
May a curse descend upon his neck,
And may his shroud burn for nothing.
Manas is Akun’s son-in-law;
And to Manas shall become a bride
Akun’s moonlike Chürök.”
“These are the heroes’ words,” they said,
And the assembled people surged in uproar.
For Chürök, daughter of Akun,
They said, “This is the feast given to the people.”
Where the great Akkan takes its source,
In broad, pine-clad Talas,
Along the banks where the people assembled,
On the plain of Üch-Kapkak,
Beside the Ukuruk,
Along the Aigyr-Jal,
At the memorial feast of Kökötöy, father of the people—
That warrior Kökötöy’s
Feast from which he would never return—
Before all the multitude,
With the people’s mightiest giants,
Bloodthirsty Manas and Er Koshoy,
And warrior Bakai at their head,
They slaughtered barren yearling colts,
Setting vodka, bozo, and costly food
Before everyone without distinction.
Er Töshtük, son of Eleman,
Jamgyrchy of the Eshtек people,
Khan Kökchö of the Kazakhs,
Chambyl and Muzburchak the fearsome—
These were chosen as impartial witnesses.
“In the high seat on Judgment Day,
Let this be a covenant for all time;
Let such great men as these
Stand as witnesses.
All who have heard, great and small,
And even the most insolent enemies,
Heed these words.”
Showing the whites of their teeth,
They slaughtered livestock fatter than horses
And divided the abundant wealth and animals received
Equally among them.
Barren yearling colts and white-gray mares
Were brought forward with the blessing;
So much wealth
Was spent and given away.
A white wether with a yellow head
Was sacrificed with a cry of “Baabedin!”
They devised wonders no man could imagine
And held a feast for all the people;
Great herds of all four kinds of livestock
Were lavishly slaughtered.
The poor and starving, beset by endless hardship,
Ate their fill at that feast.
White fat lay there like a lake,
Delighting even the eyes
Of those who merely stood and watched.
They became sacred in-laws and feasted on fat,
Gathering the people to honor her.
Such was the measure of Chürök,
Such the singular bearing of that wondrous beauty.
The people clashed and the nation stirred,
Her splendor beyond all reckoning;
The woman who was Akun’s daughter,
Whose fame stirred the people of the age,
That shimmering enchantress,
Whose magnificence lay serene.
The fame of this noble-born Chürök
Became renowned throughout the age.
Konurbai of the Kara-Kytai
Heard word of her;
That Konurbai grew frenzied,
And his whole world was shaken.
Livestock was gathered in the midst,
His foremost troops were slaughtered,
And turmoil and strife erupted there.
Her beauty became known;
All whose ears heard and eyes beheld it—
All the people were thrown into turmoil.
“If only that wondrous Aichürök
Were our wife,” they said;
Women and men alike raged like dogs,
And those dog-hearted people grieved.
The power of this wondrous Chürök’s service,
Her force and venom, were great;
Before this shimmering marvel,
Every soul in the world despaired.
“This girl is beautiful,” they said,
And the preciousness of the hapless maiden
Became known to all the peoples of the age.
Her token was every fleet thoroughbred,
A steed worthy of a karat.
Because of the poison of this vile world,
For the sake of Aichürök,
Kartküröng and Buurul, two thoroughbreds,
And the brothers Ogoy and Shygai—
From Ogoy came fierce Er Manas,
And from Khan Shygai came Chynkojo—
Through Aichürök’s fierce power,
We brothers became strangers to one another.
We lashed our pinewood spears together
And fought one another many times,
Tearing lungs and spilling gall,
Nursing grudges and severing heads,
Standing opposed and crushing each other,
Splashing blood like black water,
Pouring out all our blood,
And shattering one another’s ribs.
For the sake of the golden moon,
Through desire for the woman Aichürök,
We stood on opposing sides,
Firing guns and drawing bows,
And fought in a bloody melee.
We tore all our coats to shreds;
Every hero strained for battle,
And boundless strife arose.
We fought beyond all reckoning,
Our reason divided and our inheritance cursed,
Fighting as though drunk on fat.
